div.p: This paper advances the schedulability analysis of the Adaptive Mixed-Criticality for Weakly Hard Real-Time Systems (AMC-WH) which allows a specified number of consecutive low-criticality (LO) jobs of tasks to be skipped when the system operates in the high-criticality (HI) mode. The current AMC-WH schedulability test, based on the skip-over model, in which low tasks are guaranteed to meet m -s out of m consecutive deadlines, where s is the number of allowed skips and m is the cycle length, only calculates the worst-case response times (WCRT) for low tasks under a fixed execution pattern postmode switch. To address this limitation, we propose a new sufficient schedulability test for AMC-WH using the (m, k)-firm model, which allows various execution patterns for low tasks after a mode switch, enhancing the flexibility and applicability. Additionally, we develop an exact schedulability test for AMC-WH based on response time analysis (RTA). This test modifies the existing exact tests for the AMC algorithm, incorporating updates to state-space exploration and pruning rules to account for low task execution after a mode switch. Simulation results validate the effectiveness of our tests, demonstrating enhanced schedulability analysis and optimized resource allocation.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The concurrent execution of multiple tasks on a single hardware system poses a growing challenge in computer systems. These tasks often vary in their criticality levels, adding to the complexity. Consider, for instance, an embedded device within an aircraft where tasks like the flight control system hold a higher criticality level compared to those associated with the in-flight information system. Such intricate systems fall under the category of Mixed-Criticality (MC) systems. Broadly speaking, MC systems represent a subset of real-time systems wherein two or more criticality levels characterize tasks. The criticality assigned to tasks within MC systems is contingent upon their defined assurance levels, adhering to standards set forth by certification authorities such as IEC 61508 [1], DO-178B [2], DO-178C [3], ISO 26262 [4], and others.

Following the Vestal model [5], a well-explored framework for Mixed-Criticality (MC) systems, each task is associated with multiple Worst-Case Execution Times (WCETs), contingent on the task's criticality level. Notably, the WCET for higher criticality levels is estimated more conservatively than lower ones. The Vestal model initiates the system in a criticality mode set at the lowest level. As tasks surpass the WCET corresponding to the system's criticality mode, the system elevates its criticality by one level.

In scenarios following the model proposed by Baruah et al. [6], known as Adaptive Mixed-Criticality (AMC), tasks with lower criticality levels are halted-meaning the scheduler does not incorporate them in its scheduling. Additionally, Asyaban et al. [7] presented a precise schedulability test for AMC based on response time analysis (RTA).

Gettings et al. [8] introduced the Adaptive Mixed-Criticality Weakly Hard (AMC-WH) approach, allowing for the execution of some instances of lower criticality tasks after a criticality mode change. They provided sufficient schedulability tests using Response Time Analysis (RTA). AMC-WH employs a specific model, namely skip-over [9], for selecting jobs of lower criticality tasks, although specific applications, such as multimedia, may necessitate support for more general patterns.

MC systems must handle tasks of differing criticality levels, ensuring that high-criticality (HI) tasks receive sufficient resources "while still maintaining a certain level of service for low-criticality (LO) tasks. Traditional MC scheduling approaches often prioritize high tasks to the detriment of low tasks, potentially leading to a complete neglect of low tasks during critical system states. This trade-off, while ensuring the safety and reliability of high tasks, can severely degrade the overall system performance and user experience.

To address this issue, AMC-WH algorithm has been proposed. AMC-WH extends conventional MC scheduling by introducing weakly hard constraints, permitting a defined number of consecutive low task jobs to be skipped when the system is in high criticality mode. This adaptive strategy lowers system load, freeing resources for high tasks, while continuing to offer a reduced but acceptable level of service for low tasks. The key feature of AMC-WH is its guarantee that low tasks will meet m -s out of m deadlines, where s is the number of allowed skips within a cycle of length m.

Existing schedulability tests for the AMC-WH algorithm primarily focus on the skip-over model, which assumes a specific execution pattern for low tasks during high criticality mode. However, real-world applications may require more flexible execution patterns for low tasks after a criticality mode change, which the current tests do not accommodate. Additionally, the precise schedulability tests available for standard AMC algorithms do not account for the continued execution of low tasks post-criticality change, leading to potential inaccuracies in system analysis and planning.

This paper aims to enhance the AMC-WH algorithm on a single processor system by developing both sufficient and exact schedulability tests that incorporate various execution patterns for low tasks, modeled through the (m, k)-firm approach [10]. The (m, k)-firm model offers a more general framework than the skip-over model, allowing for a broader range of task execution scenarios and improving the accuracy of worst-case response time (WCRT) calculations. By employing the (m, k)-firm model, various combinations of m and k can be explored to assess the schedulability of tasksets under different execution patterns of low-criticality tasks in highcriticality mode.
The contributions of this paper are twofold:

• We propose a sufficient schedulability test for the AMC-WH algorithm based on the (m, k)-firm model, enabling the inclusion of diverse execution patterns for low tasks and supporting the traditional skip-over model as a special case. • We introduce an exact schedulability test for the AMC-WH algorithm, utilizing precise response time analysis and incorporating updated pruning rules to account for the execution of low tasks in high-criticality mode. Through these enhancements, we aim to provide a more robust and flexible framework for MC system scheduling, ensuring better resource allocation, improved system performance, and maintained service quality for low-criticality tasks even during high criticality mode. This work represents a significant step forward in the practical application of MC scheduling algorithms, bridging the gap between theoretical models and real-world requirement.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II provides a review of related work on the schedulability analysis of MC systems. Section III describes the system model considered in this paper. Section IV describes the proposed sufficient and exact schedulability tests for weakly hard real-time MC Systems. Section V shows the experimental results and finally, Section VI concludes the paper.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: The MC sporadic task model, introduced by Vestal in 2007 [5], forms the foundation for assigning different WCET values to tasks based on their criticality levels. In this model, tasks with higher criticality levels are given more conservative WCET estimates. The Audsley's optimal priority assignment (OPA) algorithm [11] has been demonstrated to be optimal for task priority assignment in MC systems.

In the domain of fixed-priority (FP) preemptive scheduling algorithms, Baruah et al. [6] advanced the Static Mixed-Criticality (SMC) analysis, grounded in response time analysis [12], and introduced the AMC approach. This approach is designed for systems with two criticality levels (high and low), initiating operations in low-criticality mode. If a task's execution time exceeds the WCET of the current system level, the system escalates to high-criticality mode. In this mode, low-criticality tasks are abandoned, and all high-criticality tasks execute based on their high-criticality WCET estimates.

The skip-over approach, introduced by Koren et al. in 1995 [9], provides a mechanism to skip one in every s invocations of tasks during system overloads. This method follows a fixed pattern, which limits its flexibility. Building on this, the concept of weakly hard real-time constraints [13] has been leveraged to enhance system performance. Gettings et al. [8] proposed the AMC-WH algorithm, which employs the skipover model to skip some consecutive jobs of low-criticality tasks following a system mode change. This approach prevents the complete abandonment of low-criticality jobs, ensuring a degraded but acceptable level of service.

The AMC-WH algorithm utilizes Audsley's OPA algorithm [11] for task priority assignment. Gettings et al. [8], focusing on FP scheduling and the skipping method for low-criticality tasks post-criticality mode change, introduced two sufficient schedulability tests: AMCrtb-WH and AMCmax-WH, both based on WCRT analysis. These tests calculate the WCRT of tasks across three distinct states: low-criticality mode, high-criticality mode, and during the system mode change. AMCrtb-WH obtains the WCRT of tasks by assuming that all high-criticality tasks are executed with their corresponding high-criticality WCET value before and after the mode change. AMCmax-WH determines the WCRT of tasks by considering that tasks released before the mode change have already been executed and therefore are unaffected by the mode change.

To address the limitations of existing models, Hamdaoui and Ramanathan [10] introduced the (m, k)-firm model. This model offers a more flexible framework by ensuring that for every k consecutive executions of a task, at least m must meet their deadlines. This flexibility makes the (m, k)-firm model suitable for a wide range of applications, including multimedia systems.

Asyaban et al. [7] extended the work on AMC by providing an exact schedulability test based on response time analysis. Their method accurately calculates the WCRTs for tasks, accounting for both criticality modes and the transition between them. This exact analysis improves the predictability and reliability of MC systems, ensuring that all critical tasks meet their deadlines.

This paper builds on these foundational works by proposing enhancements to the AMC-WH algorithm. We introduce both sufficient and exact schedulability tests that incorporate the (m, k)-firm model, providing greater flexibility and accuracy in scheduling lower criticality tasks during high criticality mode. Our work aims to bridge the gap between theoretical models and practical requirements, ensuring robust performance and improved service quality in MC systems.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: This section presents the system model, considering the MC sporadic task model proposed by Burns et al. [14]. We assume two criticality levels: Low and High. Each task set Π encompasses N tasks, with each task τ i defined by the following parameters:
div.formula: L i , C LO i , C HI i , T i , D i , m i , k i , where: • L i ∈ {LO, HI}: The criticality level of task τ i . • C LO i :
div.p: The WCET of task τ i at the low-criticality level. • C HI i : The WCET of task τ i at the high-criticality level. • T i : The period of task τ i .
• D i : The deadline of task τ i .

• m i : The number of jobs from task τ i inside each window that must meet their deadlines. • k i : The size of the windows. The total utilization of each task set with respect to criticality level l is defined as:
div.formula: U l = N i=1 C l i
div.p: Ti . Additionally, we define hp(i) as the set of tasks with a higher priority than τ i ; hpHI(i) and hpLO(i) as a subset of hp(i) comprising tasks with a high-criticality level and low-criticality level, respectively.

The system operates in two modes: 1) Low-Criticality Mode (LO): In this mode, all tasks are scheduled based on their low-criticality WCET (C LO i ). The system aims to ensure that every task meets its deadline under normal operating conditions. 2) High-Criticality Mode (HI): When a task exceeds its low-criticality WCET (C LO i ), the system switches to high-criticality mode. In this mode, high-criticality tasks are scheduled based on their high-criticality WCET (C HI i ), while low-criticality tasks are scheduled according to the (m, k)-firm model. To execute low-criticality tasks in the high-criticality mode, we consider the deeply-red (m,k)-pattern [15] and evenly distributed (m,k)-pattern [15]. The determination of mandatory jobs (jobs to be executed) for low-criticality task τ i based on the deeply-red (m,k)-pattern is expressed by the following equation [15]:

div.p: in which the j th job (j = 1, 2, . . . , k i ) of τ i , i.e. τ ij is mandatory if π ij = 1; otherwise, it is optional. The evenlydistributed pattern, aims to distribute mandatory jobs as evenly as possible according to the following equation:

div.head: IV. PROPOSED SCHEDULABILITY TESTS
div.p: As discussed in Section II, the schedulability test for the AMC-WH scheduling algorithm relies on the skip-over model to compute the WCRT of tasks. However, depending on the system application, other execution patterns for low-criticality tasks after a criticality mode change might be required. In such cases, the existing relations for the schedulability test cannot be applied. Additionally, the exact schedulability test for the AMC algorithm does not consider low-criticality tasks after a mode change.

This section consists of two parts. In the first part, we propose a sufficient schedulability test for the AMC-WH algorithm using the (m, k)-firm model, allowing different patterns for executing low-criticality tasks and computing their WCRT. Given that the skip-over model is equivalent to the inverse deeply-red pattern [15], the sufficient test we present also supports the skip-over model. In the second part, we propose an exact schedulability test for the AMC-WH algorithm using the skip-over model, considering low-criticality tasks after a mode change. This exact test is based on response time analysis, incorporating modifications from the exact schedulability test for the AMC algorithm, along with revised and new pruning rules.

A. Sufficient schedulability test using the (m, k)-firm model As discussed in Section II, the sufficient schedulability tests for the AMC-WH algorithm assume low-criticality tasks are executed according to the skip-over model after a mode change. Since these tests are based on a specific model, they cannot be applied to different patterns for executing low-criticality tasks. Therefore, we introduce a more general model, the (m, k)-firm model, and present relations based on AMCrtb-WH and AMCmax-WH tests. These relations allow considering any pattern for low-criticality tasks after a mode change and computing their WCRT.

The new sufficient schedulability tests use a function f p (n i ) to indicate whether the n-th job of a low-criticality task τ i is executed at time t according to the pattern p. If we use the deeply-red pattern, the function f p (n i ) is defined as:

div.head: B. Exact schedulability test
div.p: In the AMC-WH scheduling algorithm, low-criticality tasks are usually ignored after a mode change to reduce system overload and prioritize high-criticality tasks. However, this can degrade system quality. The AMC-WH algorithm addresses this by servicing some low-criticality jobs to maintain system quality while reducing the workload by skipping some lowcriticality jobs.

We propose an exact schedulability test for the AMC-WH algorithm, assuming low-criticality tasks are executed according to the skip-over model in the high-criticality mode. This test is based on the exact schedulability test for the AMC algorithm, updated to support low-criticality tasks. The pseudocode for the exact schedulability test is shown in Algorithm 1.

Algorithm 1. Exact schedulability test for AMC-WH Input: Π = {τ 1 , ..., τ N } , | for all tasks τ i ∈ Π, priority order P r(τ i ) = i; Output: R k for all tasks τ k ∈ Π, if Π is schedulable; null, otherwise;
div.formula: 1 for each τ k ∈ Π do 2 if ∀τ j ∈ {τ i , ..., τ k } , C LO j == C HI j then 3 R k = C LO k + j<k R k T j C LO j ; 4 else if ∀τ j ∈ {τ 1 , ..., τ k } , L j == L k then 5 R k = C L k k + j<k R k T j C L k j ; 6 else 7 R k = SB -RT A(Π, k); 8 if R k > D k then 9
div.p: return null; 10 return {R 1 , ..., R k }

In Algorithm 1, if the first two conditions (Lines 2 and 4) are not met, the algorithm enters the state tree construction phase. Function SB -RT A calculates R k by examining all possible MC instances (Line 7). Considering the system states generated, low-criticality tasks are also included after a mode change. The function SB -RT A explores different possible states of the tasks to find the WCRT. At each time point t, the system state is defined as
div.formula: s t = ⟨Γ, (c i , q i , p i , ϵ i ) N
div.p: i=1 ⟩, where:

• Γ ∈ {LO, HI} indicates the current criticality mode of the system. • For each task τ i , c i ∈ {0, . . . , C HI i } represents the remaining worst-case execution time of its current pending job. q i ∈ {0, . . . , D i } is the time left until the deadline of its last job. p i ∈ {0, . . . , T i } denotes the minimum remaining time until the next release of τ i . ϵ i ∈ {0, . . . , C HI i } is the worst actual execution time of the pending job of task τ i . In our proposed method, we utilize the exact schedulability test developed in [7] to ensure the schedulability of MC systems. This test is grounded in identifying the critical instant and the worst-case scenario that impacts the schedulability of a task set.

The critical instant is the point at which a task set's schedulability is most challenged. Asyaban et al. define this as the simultaneous arrival sequence of tasks. The worst-case scenario is constructed by considering all possible behaviors of the system. However, due to state space explosion, only the worst-case features are considered to make the problem tractable.

In the context of mode changes, low-criticality tasks are discarded after a mode change. The test assumes that the system will transition to a high-criticality mode under certain conditions, impacting the schedulability of low-criticality tasks. high-criticality tasks' response times and schedulability are analyzed considering that they might have carry-in jobs (jobs released before the mode change but completing after).

Considering the execution of low-criticality tasks in highcriticality mode, the algorithm may be exponential. To reduce the state space, the exact schedulability test employs pruning rules. These rules eliminate states that do not contribute to the worst-case scenario, thus optimizing the analysis process. The schedulability test involves checking if any task misses its deadline in the worst-case scenario. If no deadlines are missed, the system is deemed schedulable. The test leverages the WCRT analysis for this purpose.

By incorporating these concepts from [7], our method ensures a rigorous and comprehensive analysis of MC systems. This approach not only validates the schedulability of tasks under varying criticality levels but also optimizes the analysis process through effective state space pruning 1 .

1) New pruning rules: New pruning rules are introduced to reduce the state space search, ensuring that low-criticality tasks are considered after a mode change. The updated pruning rules are as follows:

• Prune Rule 1**: If the system is currently in high criticality mode (Γ = HI) and there exists a low-criticality task τ i for i ∈ {1, 2, . . . , k -1} such that p i ≤ 0, then the state can be pruned. • Prune Rule 2**: If there exists a low-criticality task τ i for i ∈ {m + 1, . . . , k -1} such that p i ≤ 0 and C LO m + s i T i ≥ q k , then the state can be pruned.
• Prune Rule 3**: If a high-criticality task τ m ′ with the lowest priority among higher-priority tasks of τ m exists, and

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we evaluate the proposed schedulability tests using various patterns according to the (m, k)-firm model. We examine the results by varying different parameters and assess their impact on the schedulability of task sets using the proposed exact schedulability test. Additionally, we compare the performance of different priority assignment algorithms, including OPA [16], DM [17], and NOPA [7]. The implementation of the schedulability tests was conducted in MATLAB on a hardware platform with the following specifications: an Intel Core i3-7100 3.90GHz processor and 8.00 GB of RAM.

div.head: A. Task set generation
div.p: Task sets were randomly generated using the UUniFast algorithm [18]. The utilization of the task sets was generated in steps of 0.1, ranging from 0.05 to 0.95. Task periods were sampled from a log-uniform distribution between 10 and 100. The WCET of tasks in low-criticality mode, denoted as C LO i for each task τ i , was calculated by multiplying the task's utilization by its period. The WCET for high-criticality tasks was generated as C HI i = CF × C LO i , where CF > 1 (the criticality factor) represents the ratio of high-criticality WCET to low-criticality WCET. The criticality level of each task was randomly generated based on a parameter, 0 < P HI < 1, which indicates the proportion of high-criticality tasks.

For the evaluations, 500 task sets were generated with the assumption that D i = T i . By default, each task set consisted of 5 tasks with CF = 2, P HI = 0.5, m = 1, and k = 2 for low-criticality tasks. However, the results are presented for varying values of utilization (from 0.05 to 0.95 in steps of 0.1), CF (from 1 to 5 in steps of 1), P HI (from 0.5 to 0.9 in steps of 0.1), and m (from 0 to 5 in steps of 1).

div.head: B. Evaluation of sufficient schedulability tests
div.p: This section presents the results obtained from the sufficient schedulability tests applied using different patterns. The optimal priority assignment algorithm (OPA) was used for task priority assignment.

Fig. 1a, Fig. 1b, and Fig. 1c show the results of the AMCrtb-WH and AMCmax-WH tests using the deeply-red and its inverse patterns. Fig. 2a and Fig. 2b also show the results for evenly distributed pattern (namely E-pattern in the figure) and its inverse. The weighted schedulability metric [19] was used as a function of various variables, calculated as follows: Since the AMCrtb-WH test considers the WCRT pessimistically, its graph lies below the AMCmax-WH test graph in all figures, indicating fewer tasks are schedulable. Additionally, tests using the inverse deeply-red pattern showed higher schedulability compared to the deeply-red pattern. This is because, in high-criticality mode, executing low-criticality tasks from the end of the window allows the tasks seeking the WCRT to complete their execution with less interference.

div.p: In Fig. 1b, increasing the criticality factor decreases schedulability due to the increased system load. Similarly, in Fig. 1c, higher P HI values increase the likelihood of having more high-criticality tasks in a set, reducing schedulability as system load increases in high-criticality mode. Fig. 2a and Fig. 2b show results for k = 5 with varying m values. When k = 5, for m = 1 and m = 4, both inverse deeply-red and inverse evenly distributed patterns yield similar results. This occurs because, for m = 1 and m = 4, the jobs of tasks chosen based on both of these patterns are identical. For m = 2 and m = 3, the inverse deeply-red pattern provides better schedulability than the evenly distributed pattern. When using normal patterns, the evenly distributed pattern, which distributes the mandatory jobs as evenly as possible, offers better schedulability due to its balanced distribution.

div.head: C. Evaluation of exact schedulability test
div.p: This section evaluates the introduced exact schedulability test using the skip-over model.

1) Performance: We evaluate the execution time of the proposed exact schedulability test and compare it with other tests. Various priority assignment strategie, such as NOPA and DM, are used for this comparison. Fig. 3a and Fig. 3b show the execution time of the proposed test with NOPA and DM priority assignment algorithms for varying criticality factors. Increasing the criticality factor increases execution time due to more states being generated in the state tree. Fig. 4a and Fig. 4b show the execution time with varying P HI. With higher P HI values, the execution time increases, as does the utilization.

2) Schedulability: This section evaluates the effectiveness of the NOPA, DM, and OPA priority assignment algorithms using the proposed exact schedulability test, the exact schedulability test for the AMC algorithm, and the sufficient AMCmax-WH test. The AMCmax-WH test is compatible with the OPA algorithm, whereas the exact tests are not. Hence, the combination of the exact schedulability test and the OPA algorithm is not included. Since the skip-over model is used, m represents the number of jobs in each cycle, and s denotes the number of skips.

Fig. 5a shows the results of various schedulability tests. The graph for the exact schedulability test for the AMC algorithm is above the proposed test, indicating that including lowcriticality tasks after a mode change increases system load and decreases schedulability. Conversely, the proposed exact test's graph is above the sufficient AMCmax-WH test graph due to its pessimistic nature. Without the skip-over model, the NOPA algorithm performs better than DM. However, with the skip-over model, DM performs better, as NOPA assigns lower priorities to low-criticality tasks. In Fig. 5b, increasing the criticality factor decreases schedulability across all tests due to higher WCET values for high-criticality tasks. Similarly, in Fig. 5c, higher P HI values decrease schedulability due to more high-criticality tasks. In Fig. 5d, with m = 3, increasing s slightly improves schedulability.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we provided sufficient schedulability tests for the AMC-WH scheduling algorithm based on the WCRT analysis using the (m, k)-firm model for different patterns. The results showed that the inverse deeply-red pattern provided better schedulability than the inverse evenly distributed pattern, while the evenly distributed pattern offered better schedulability than the deeply-red pattern. We also proposed an exact schedulability test considering low-criticality tasks after a mode change using the skip-over model and evaluated the results. The DM priority assignment algorithm performed better with the proposed exact test, whereas NOPA performed better with the exact test for the AMC algorithm.
